common_name: Samoan Fluff Plumeria (White Yellow-Throated Fragrant Plumeria)

planting.note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Samoan Fluff (also sold as Tahitian White) bears wide, heavily overlapping white petals around a small greenish-yellow center with light pink banding on the reverse.

directions: Root cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun after allowing the cut end to callus for one to two weeks. Samoan Fluff produces large, full, rounded flowers of good substance with wide, round-tipped petals that overlap heavily, giving the bloom a plush, layered appearance around a brilliant greenish-yellow throat brushed with faint pink on the back of the petals. A moderate, steady bloomer from spring through fall, it holds its color and form in the lei well and resists the yellowing that affects some older white cultivars. As with other Plumeria rubra hybrids, plants go fully deciduous and dormant in winter and must be kept completely dry during that rest period; in zone 9a, overwinter bare-root or containerized plants indoors in a frost-free, unwatered location and return them outdoors once new growth resumes in spring.

common_name: Pauahi Ali'i Plumeria (Fragrant Gold-and-Red Hawaiian Plumeria)

planting.note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Pauahi Ali'i is a Hawaiian-named cultivar with narrow, slightly overlapping golden petals streaked in red and orange and a mild lemon fragrance.

directions: Plant callused cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun. Pauahi Ali'i is a medium-growing Hawaiian cultivar prized for its warm, tropical mix of golden-yellow petals streaked and flushed with red and orange toward the base, carried on narrow, slightly overlapping petals with a light, sweet, lemony fragrance. It is a consistent mid-season to late-season bloomer that holds its multicolor pattern well in cut arrangements. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids it drops its leaves and enters full winter dormancy in cool weather and must be kept bone-dry through that rest; in zone 9a, overwinter container specimens in a frost-free, unwatered spot and resume watering only after new growth appears in spring. Excellent drainage year-round prevents stem and root rot.
sources: Hawaii Plumeria Society — Named Cultivar Registry

planting.note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Penang Peach is a compact, low-growing cultivar introduced from Malaysia's Penang Island bearing thick, apricot-peach flowers with a cocoa-and-cinnamon fragrance.

directions: Root cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; the compact, low-branching growth habit of Penang Peach makes it well suited to container culture and easy flower picking. Introduced to Hawaii from Malaysia's Penang Island, this cultivar produces thick-petaled, three-inch, apricot-peach flowers edged in soft pink that shift toward reddish tones in hot weather and brighten to clearer yellow in cooler conditions, released with a rich, sweet cocoa-and-cinnamon fragrance that makes it a favorite for lei making. Leaves carry a distinctive hooked tip and reddish margins. As with other Plumeria rubra hybrids, the tree is winter-deciduous and must be kept completely dry through dormancy; in zone 9a, overwinter container plants in a frost-free, unwatered location and resume watering once new growth emerges in spring.

common_name: Scott Pratt Plumeria (Dark Red-Black Fragrant Plumeria)

planting.note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Scott Pratt was the first plumeria cultivar ever formally registered and bears narrow, deep red-black petals with a spicy cinnamon fragrance.

directions: Plant callused cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; upright, thin-stemmed trees benefit from staking while young. Scott Pratt, historically significant as the first plumeria cultivar ever formally registered and named for the Kohala Sugar Plantation's farm manager, produces abundant narrow, elliptical, moderately overlapping petals in a color so deeply saturated red it reads nearly black in hot weather, with fine dark radiating lines around a small red center and a strong, spicy cinnamon fragrance. It is a prolific, nearly year-round bloomer in warm climates. Like other Plumeria rubra hybrids it is winter-deciduous and must be kept completely dry through dormancy; in zone 9a, overwinter container specimens in a frost-free, unwatered location and resume watering only after new growth resumes in spring.

common_name: Irma Bryan Plumeria (Velvety Red Fragrant Plumeria)

planting.note: Allow cuttings to dry and callus for 1-2 weeks before planting in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; Irma Bryan is a robust, umbrella-shaped cultivar and one of the earliest red plumerias to flower each season, bearing deep velvety red blooms with a spicy fragrance.

directions: Root cuttings in extremely well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; give this medium to tall, umbrella-shaped grower ample room to spread. Irma Bryan is among the earliest red plumerias to bloom each season, producing wide, elliptical, moderately overlapping petals of deep velvety red with prominent darker red veins and wavy edges surrounding a small orange-yellow center, released with a mild spicy fragrance that strengthens as cut flowers are stored. New foliage emerges tinged with dark red anthocyanin before maturing green. As with other Plumeria rubra hybrids, the tree drops its leaves and goes fully dormant in cool weather and must be kept completely dry through that rest period; in zone 9a, overwinter container plants in a frost-free, unwatered spot and resume watering once new growth appears in spring.
